title: The shortest great sutra
hookLine: a short Mahayana text chanted daily across East Asia, spoken by Avalokiteshvara (Heart Sutra)
tomorrow: form is emptiness. how can one cup be empty and full at once?

cards: Some weeks you get through on one sentence said over and over: it's going to be okay, one more day, breathe. The Chinese monk Xuanzang, on his long road to India, had a whole text that worked like that.
His biography says that before the journey west he found a sick man in rags, covered in sores, and took him in, fed him and clothed him. In thanks, the man taught him a short sutra.
Later, alone in the desert, when terrifying shapes rose around him, Xuanzang recited it, and they were gone. The text was the Heart Sutra.

teach.b: It's short, and its full name calls it the heart of the Perfection of Wisdom, a much larger body of Mahayana teaching. Here's how it opens.
Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, is deep in the practice of perfect wisdom.

He looks closely at what a person is made of, the five heaps: body, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness. And he sees that all five are empty. Then the sutra says he crossed beyond all suffering.
Then a surprise. He teaches this to Shariputra, the disciple known for wisdom in the older teachings.
The wise one is being taught by the compassionate one.
Mahayana teachers often read the scene this way: wisdom and compassion aren't two paths. A bodhisattva sees clearly so that he can help, and helps by seeing clearly.
In Zen, Chan and other Mahayana communities, this little text is chanted in many languages, often together. Xuanzang's story fits it.
He took in a man covered in sores, and that act of compassion handed him the wisdom he'd need in the desert. The sutra doesn't promise the desert goes away. It says suffering can be crossed.

how: Mahayana Buddhists in China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and beyond chant the Heart Sutra in their own languages, often together in temples and at services.

games.q: what does “the shortest great sutra” mean?
o: a short blessing said before a Buddhist meal
a short text holding the core of perfect wisdom
the Buddha's long first sermon to five monks

games.q: who's who in the Heart Sutra: tap the pairs.
p: recited it alone in the desert

s: the Heart Sutra is a lucky charm that makes problems go away
it teaches that the five heaps are empty and suffering can be crossed. Xuanzang still had to cross the desert.
in the sutra, the wise disciple Shariputra is the one being taught
Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, teaches him.
the sutra's 'empty' means that nothing matters
Avalokiteshvara sees the five heaps are empty and crosses beyond suffering, out of compassion. a lot matters.

games.q: your friend is going through a hard week and asks what the Heart Sutra is actually 'for.' what do you say?
o: seeing clearly, out of compassion, so suffering can be crossed.
keeping bad luck away, like a charm you say for protection.
proving nothing matters, so you stop caring about the hard week.
games.why: Avalokiteshvara sees the heaps are empty and crosses beyond suffering. in Mahayana teaching, wisdom and compassion go together.

practice: If you can, play a recording of the Heart Sutra chanted, in any language, and just listen: the rhythm, the breath, the voices together.
If you can't, listen to the steadiest sound around you, a fan, traffic, your own breathing, and let it carry you the way a chant carries the people who say it.

wordCard.voice: The shortest great sutra: a name some readers give the Heart Sutra, a short text at the core of the Perfection of Wisdom, spoken by the bodhisattva of compassion.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the heart of the perfection of wisdom, the Heart Sutra's name.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the heart sutra, a short text of wisdom for crossing suffering. Day 1482, done.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita Hridaya), opening (Avalokiteshvara, practicing the deep perfection of wisdom, sees the five aggregates are empty and crosses beyond all suffering; addressed to Shariputra)
Huili, The Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, book 1 (the sick man who teaches him the sutra; reciting it in the desert)
